speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: COTTON TEXTILES-IMPOSITION OF EXPORT QUOTAS BY HONG KONG
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house will recall that an international short term arrangement on trade in cotton textiles was negotiated in Geneva last July. Canada signed the arrangement on September 5 and it came into force on October 1, for a period of one year. On February 16 I tabled in the house a copy of a long term arrangement which was being submitted to the governments of participating countries for approval. It is envisaged that the long term arrangement would come into effect on October 1 of this year, when the short term arrangement expires.
These arrangements are aimed at expanding the export opportunities of less developed countries, while at the same time preventing disruption in the domestic markets of importing countries.
Hong Kong is a substantial supplier of very low cost cotton textile goods to Canada. Early this year there was a noticeable increase in Hong Kong's exports to Canada of one important category, cotton slacks and shorts. The colony's exports of this category to Canada had more than doubled between 1958 and 1959. They then increased by a further 80 per cent in 1960 to a level of about 300,000 dozen. This was, by quantity, about 18 per cent of the total market. In 1961 there was a slight decline, which was part of the general falling off in Hong Kong's exports of textiles to Canada. However, shipments of cotton slacks and shorts in December and in January of this year gave every 26207-1-155
indication that exports would rise rapidly and cause further disruption in the Canadian market.
In February the Canadian government requested Hong Kong to impose export restraints under the terms of the short term arrangement. This arrangement provides that an importing country may request an exporting country to apply restraints at a level not lower than actual shipments in the year ended June 30, 1961. Last week Mr. H. A. Angus, director of Hong Kong's department of commerce and industry, visited Ottawa and held discussions with Canadian government officials. As a result of these discussions Hong Kong has agreed to impose export restraints, in accordance with the provisions of the Geneva agreement, totalling 255,000 dozen cotton slacks and shorts, divided as follows: men's 70,000 dozen; women's, 55,000 dozen; children's, 130,000 dozen, for the period ending October 1, 1962.
The United States government has also requested Hong Kong to impose restraints on exports of a number of cotton textile items. On March 19 the United States government announced that it would prohibit the importation for consumption of certain shipments from Hong Kong. This naturally gave rise to some concern in Canada lest large quantities of goods ordered for the United States market be diverted to our market. This possibility was discussed with the visiting Hong Kong officials in connection with their future licensing arrangements. Both sides agreed that it was unlikely that serious problems of this kind would arise for Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ADDITIONAL ONTARIO JUDGES
speechtext: I thank the minister for clarifying the matter. I think if he reexamines his remarks of yesterday he will find an ambiguity in them which I think it is desirable to have clarified for the record. That is all I was seeking to do.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rather anticipated when I saw the bill that it would make provision for special remuneration for a chief county court judge. As the hon. member for Ottawa West said yesterday, that is rather unsatisfactory. I thought the hon. member made a very good comparison in this respect. Another salary range is between $12,000 and $14,000, and there are 15 who in the normal course of salary increases, based on relatively short term service, rise to a salary of $12,000.
I thought this was a very telling point in favour of a reconsideration of the present salary offered to county and district court judges in Ontario as presented yesterday by the hon. member for Ottawa West. It was pointed out in the Ontario house, I think, that all these judges would normally carry out surrogate court work and would receive a remuneration of $1,500 from the province, but there was considerable vagueness about some of these other opportunities to which the Minister of Justice referred yesterday. The minister indicated that this matter is under review, but I also read that these gentlemen had a spokesman about three weeks ago, Judge Cooper of Sudbury, who indicated that he thought they were very dissatisfied with their place in life. As I say, I merely wish to endorse in every way what the hon. member for Ottawa West said yesterday as to their importance in the judicial system. It is all the more important in areas such as the one I represent, where we have two district courts and where we very seldom, because of distance, have an opportunity to receive judicial decisions from a higher level such as the supreme court of Ontario. As a consequence litigants on both
Judges Act

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ADDITIONAL ONTARIO JUDGES
speechtext: I do not think there is any need to prolong this discussion. subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ADDITIONAL ONTARIO JUDGES

because it introduced a bill into that legislature is necessarily going to be successful in having that bill passed.

Well, the hon. gentleman a moment ago, when he asked not to be interrupted, suggested that these interruptions were a waste of time. I would remind the hon. gentleman of his own recipe.
As I was saying when I was interrupted by the Minister of Justice, this legislation cannot have any validity until the Ontario legislature has acted. We do not know how it is going to act. Indeed, in the present disturbed state of opinion in the province of Ontario it is quite possible that that legislature may be dissolved long before this parliament is, without any more legislation being passed, and therefore it is presumptuous of us to assume that that legislature will act. In doing so we are taking them for granted; we are assuming the legislature is going to do something it may never do.
I say, sir, that this bill should never have been introduced at all until the Ontario legislature had acted. This legislation could then have been introduced and it would have been passed very quickly, because there has never been any hold up on these bills once the legislature has acted. There is only one reason why the government is trying to slip this thing through at this stage. I can think of only one reason, but I will not seek to discuss it at this point because anyone can well imagine what it is. But the real point is that the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and the leader of the house have time after time said that the members of the opposition were obstructing and holding up urgent business in this house by debating the millions and millions and millions they are spending. They have said that in discussing the estimates we have been holding up urgent business. I say that is urgent business in this house; this is not urgent yet, until the Ontario legislature has acted.
When the government suspend the consideration of the expenditures for the last fiscal year, what urgent business do they bring before us? They present a hypothetical piece of legislation that can have no effect until the Ontario legislature has acted, if it decides to act. That is the most urgent thing they can think of to bring before this parliament

now, something that cannot possibly come into effect until the legislature has acted. For that they put off consideration of supply, consideration of the budget and consideration of measures over which this parliament has some control.
I think it needs to be underlined that this is the government's idea of what is urgent business. Now, what possible benefit can it be to the government to get this legislation passed now? It can only be of benefit if they want to be sure in case the Ontario legislature does act, which we do not know anything about until it has acted, that they have a little bit of patronage. That can be their only reason for trying to rush this thing through. If they have some intention of terminating the life of this parliament they might wish to get this legislation passed before the Ontario legislature has acted so they can have the patronage during the rest of their very short life as a government.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE CANADIAN AIRCRAFT REGISTRY
speechtext:
This is probably the closest I shall get to the cabinet this session, but I certainly appreciate the honour and the suggestion of the hon. member.
This bill dealing with a central aircraft registry is one which I introduced during the past session as Bill No. C-37. It is a matter of considerable importance to the people in the aviation industry and because it is a measure of a somewhat technical nature I propose at this time to supplement the remarks I made on that occasion. I should like to refer any hon. member who is interested in this subject, and who wishes to look back, to the remarks I made then as recorded in Hansard, volume 7 at pages 7337-7343.
The purpose and principle of the bill is relatively simple, namely the establishment of a central aircraft registry to record title to and charges against Canadian civil aircraft, aircraft engines, propellers and spare parts. One of the most important aspects of the bill deals with the financing of aircraft, which is related to the degree of title protection which a finance agency may obtain on the security of an aircraft. In order to supplement the remarks I made in my previous speech on this subject, I should like to refer to a draft brief which has, I understand, been submitted informally to the Department of Transport and which was drawn up by Mr. Frank Kennerley, a lawyer who specializes in aeronautical matters and who has had a great deal of experience in aviation law. The brief will require the approval of the Canadian Bar Association, the air industries and transport association of Canada and of the industrial development bank, but I propose to refer to some of the factual historical background which is provided very concisely in the brief. This, I think, will be of interest to hon. members and also to the Minister of Transport.

Aeronautics Act
In this brief Mr. Kennerley says:
The certificate of registration for a Canadian aircraft issued by the Department of Transport is misleading to the uninformed and does not mean that the "owner" thereon named has clear legal title to the aircraft.
I think this is important, because I wrote to all of the provincial attorneys general and in the reply from the province of Quebec, I believe it was, it was indicated there was already a registration procedure established. That is correct, but it deals only with the registration of aircraft and has nothing to do with encumbrances. I continue to read:
In fact, the purchaser under a conditional sales contract, who has no legal title to the aircraft, is named on the certificate of registration as the "owner" and is so defined in the air regulations.
The finance agency must, after it is satisfied that the aircraft title is clear, also protect its prior claim in the aircraft title from subsequent purchasers, mortgagees and creditors of the owner.
The interest of title to an aircraft is therefore twofold. First, those persons who are concerned with what, if any, prior liens or encumbrances in the form of chattel mortgages, conditional sales contracts, and so on affect the title to the aircraft. Second, those persons who are concerned with the registration or giving notice to subsequent purchasers, mortgagees or creditors of prior interest in the title to the aircraft.
These interested parties must search in all common law provinces of Canada where the aircraft may have been for any registered encumbrances against the aircraft. The log book of the aircraft is of some assistance in determining where to search, but log books are not always accurate, and if a fraud is to be perpetrated, the fraudulent person is unlikely to disclose in the log book that the aircraft was ever located at the place where the encumbrance is registered. A proper search for encumbrances would involve searching every country where the aircraft may have been in every common law province that did not have a central registry. The search would be somewhat easier in those common law provinces where a central registry was located. Failure to make such a complete search may result in the aircraft landing at a distant airport only to be repossessed or seized under an encumbrance registered in the county or province where the airport is located. It is obvious that great time and expense is involved in making such a proper search. Even after completing such an exhaustive and expensive title search, the aircraft title may still be affected by an encumbrance in Quebec that is not required to be registered.
How may a finance agency protect its interest, as secured by a chattel mortgage or conditional sales contract, in a Canadian aircraft against the rights of subsequent purchasers, mortgagees or creditors?
Each of the nine common law provinces of Canada has by legislation provided for the registration of chattel mortgages and conditional sales contracts. In some provinces registration is made in the county where the aircraft is situate at the time and must be made within a limited time after the date of the transaction. This registration is effective notice to subsequent purchasers, mortgagees and, in some instances, creditors of the person in possession of the aircraft, provided the aircraft is not moved out of the county where the registration was made.

I emphasize the word "provided".
The common law provinces of British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Alberta have established one central registry for the province to include aircraft so that the registration of the encumbrance is similarly protected, provided the aircraft does not leave the province. Newfoundland is in a similar position as there is only one registry for encumbrances for the whole of the province.
All of the common law provinces have legislative provisions for the reregistration of chattel mortgages and conditional sales contracts when the aircraft is moved. In some cases where there is not a central provincial registry, from one county to another in the same province, and in all cases where the aircraft is moved from one province to another. The time limit for such reregistration varies from 20 days to two months, and in some provinces the time runs from when the mortgagee or conditional seller receives notice of the removal of the aircraft; in other provinces the time for reregistration runs from the time the aircraft is moved notwithstanding the mortgagee or conditional seller did not know about the move.
The province of Quebec, although not a common law province, has provision for registration locally throughout that province for encumbrances in certain instances. In other instances there is no provision for registration and the rights of the holder of the encumbrance against a third party are not impaired if the aircraft is purchased by the third party without notice of the prior encumbrance.
The finance agency, to protect its interest in the aircraft secured by a chattel mortgage or conditional sales contract, must follow the movement of the aircraft and register its security in accordance with the particular laws of the province where the aircraft is from time to time located. Failure to do so may result in loss of its interest in the aircraft.
A further difficulty is encountered in that the registration of chattel mortgages and conditional sales contracts must be renewed after periods varying from one to three years depending on the province of registration.
An example of the present situation in Canada would be if an aircraft is sold to an operator based at Malton airport, the seller taking a chattel mortgage from the purchaser as security, and registers the chattel mortgage in the county of Peel where Malton airport is located. Unknown to the conditional seller, the aircraft is moved to Toronto island airport and remains there for a few months during which time the purchaser goes into bankruptcy. The Toronto island airport is situate in the county of York and the relevant law of Ontario requires that the chattel mortgage must be registered in the county of York within two months after the aircraft is moved there. The failure to reregister in the county of York results in the seller who held the chattel mortgage losing that security and only being able to claim in the bankruptcy as an unsecured creditor.
Another example that has actually occurred recently was the case of an aircraft based at Winnipeg that was flown to Ontario and left in Ontario as security for charter services rendered. About three months after the aircraft had arrived in Ontario the finance agency, which held a chattel mortgage registered in Winnipeg, discovered that the aircraft had been moved to Ontario, at which time it was too late to reregister the chattel mortgage in Ontario. The finance agency, as a result, lost its security in the aircraft.
I should like to point out, as I did in the speech I made last June, that the suggestions I make with regard to this proposed central

aircraft registry have the approval of the Canadian bar. I believe there were resolutions in 1956, 1957 and 1958 to this effect.

I would prefer to get everything on the record if I could. I should like to answer questions at the end.
During the last part of my speech on June 30 of last year I spoke of a letter I had sent to the various provincial attorneys general based on my opinion that this matter was purely one of federal jurisdiction; but there was some possibility, since it dealt with encumbrances and chattel mortgages within the provinces, that it might come within the purview of provincial rights. Therefore I directed a letter to each of the attorneys general of the ten provinces drawing attention to the bill I was introducing and asking for their comments. On June 30 last as reported in Hansard of that date I read out in complete detail the replies I received from British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec and New Brunswick.
Subsequent to my bill being discussed in the house on June 30 last I have received two further replies and following my procedure of endeavouring to put the matter on the record in as complete form as possible I wish now to read the replies received from Saskatchewan and Nova Scotia. I might point out that in the correspondence reference is made to Bill No. C-37 as it was known in the previous session. The same measure is now known as Bill No. C-35.
The first is a letter from Hon. R. A. Walker, attorney general of Saskatchewan under date of June 28, 1961:
Dear Mr. Drysdale:
Re: Bill C-37
I have been considering your proposed amendment to the Aeronautics Act.
In so far as this is a matter relating to aeronautics, it falls outside the responsibility of this government and I would prefer not to make any comment.
It does appear to me, however, that if this bill is enacted it might conflict with provincial legislation governing conditional sales, bills of sale, chattel mortgages and the registration of these documents. As your bill lacks a number of the provisions presently existing in provincial legislation with respect to such matters it would not cover the area as comprehensively. I would therefore be pleased to have your views as to whether your amendment would override provincial legislation presently in force affecting instruments of title to aircraft. If you consider that it would so override, I would invite you to consider the legislation of the various provinces on this subject with a view to incorporating some of the provisions not found in your amendment.
Yours sincerely,
R. A. Walker, Attorney General.
Aeronautics Act
Under date of July 4, 1961 I received the following reply from Hon. R. A. Donahoe, attorney general of Nova Scotia:
Dear Sir:
Re Bill C-37
I have your letter of the 6th June, and had previously received your letter of the 6th April which had been referred to the departmental staff for their consideration and recommendation.
In fact, we have no provision in Nova Scotia for the registration of aircraft, and there has been no proposal that we should institute legislation providing for such registration or for the registration of encumbrances against aircraft as such. In the absence of such specific legislation, I presume that in appropriate circumstances our bills of sale act or conditional sales act would apply to aircraft.
Further to the above, I can only add that I am personally in sympathy with the general concept of a central registry for aircraft and encumbrances against aircraft, and I am confident that any request from the federal government for legislation complementary to any federal enactment would be well received in this province.
Yours very truly,
R. A. Donahoe
I should point out too, Mr. Speaker, that up to the present time I have not received a reply from Prince Edward Island or Newfoundland, but with the two replies I have just read I have now received replies from the other eight provinces.
After I made my comments in the previous debate the hon. member for Laurier, the former minister of transport in the Liberal government, offered some very constructive criticism of the proposed legislation. I wish to place on the record a comment made by the hon. member for Laurier as reported at page 7344 of volume 7 of Hansard for the 1960-61 session. The hon. gentleman stated:
That is why I think we should have two things so far as this bill is concerned. First, as is customary we should have the opinion of the minister. What does the Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) think about this legislation? Second, we should be informed whether or not the Minister of Transport has submitted the bill to the Department of Justice to ascertain whether or not it is an infringement of property and civil rights.
I put on the record in the previous debate a considerable amount of material and the hon. member for Laurier said he had some difficulty following it. I should like to refer to the fact that the letter dated April 15, 1959 from the former minister of transport, the hon. member for Broadview, is to be found at page 7339 of the same volume of Hansard. With respect to the jurisdictional aspect he said that in relying on an opinion from the Department of Justice the legislation was within the jurisdiction of parliament.
Supplementing these observations I wish now to read an exchange of correspondence between myself and the Minister of Justice

Aeronautics Act
and the Minister of Transport. I regret having to put on the record so much correspondence and detail but I feel it is the most constructive way of providing for the utmost circulation of the material I am about to present at this time.
Under date of June 30, 1961, I received the following letter from the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada:
Dear John:
I acknowledge with thanks your letter of May 20th forwarding to me a copy of a letter you have received from the attorney general of Ontario, Mr. Roberts, suggesting that your Bill C-37, entitled an act to amend the Aeronautics Act, be placed by me on the agenda of the commissioners on uniformity of legislation for discussion this summer.
This group was meeting, I believe, in Winnipeg, just prior to the annual meeting of the Canadian Bar Association. I continue:
As I understand your bill its intention is to provide for a central registry for the recording of title to, and encumbrances on, aircraft registered in Canada. The establishment of such a registry would seem to me to be a matter within the jurisdiction of parliament and not of the provincial legislatures, and I would therefore suggest that you discuss with my colleague the Minister of Transport the feasibility of his department establishing such a central registry for aircraft.
So far as the commissioners on uniformity of legislation are concerned, the principal function of that body is to recommend uniform provincial legislation, and under the rules of procedure adopted by the commissioners a few years ago matters are not ordinarily placed on the agenda unless there is reasonable likelihood that any model act prepared by the commissioners will be adopted by at least three provinces. Since the subject matter of the bill under discussion falls within federal rather than provincial jurisdiction, it would not seem to be appropriate to refer this to the commissioners.
Yours sincerely,
Davie Fulton
I received that letter on July 13. Under date of July 14, 1961 I wrote to the Minister of Justice as follows:
Dear Davie,
Thank you very much for your letter of 30 June 1961 concerning the central aircraft registry. You are quite correct that the matter is within federal jurisdiction or competence. However, the registration of encumbrances on aircraft is within provincial jurisdiction also, and it appeared to me that it would be extremely valuable to have provincial government reaction or comments on such a registry before it was established because they can insist on continuing provincial registration requirements. In fact, there would have to be legislation passed in each province stating specifically that registration in the central aircraft registry was sufficient and that registration in provincial registries was no longer necessary.
It is for the reason of notifying the provincial attorneys general that I thought this matter should be placed before the uniformity commissioners, in order to get their reaction and the necessary

provincial co-operation. Would it be possible, therefore, to bring this matter before the commissioners to obtain provincial reaction to the central aircraft registry?
Yours sincerely,
John A. W. Drysdale.
On August 3, 1961 the Minister of Justice replied to my letter as follows:
Dear John:
Thank you for your letter of July 14th setting forth your further views as to why you feel your Bill C-37, entitled an act to amend the Aeronautics Act, should be placed before the commissioners on the uniformity of legislation this summer.
It is my understanding that apart from possibly the conditional sales acts there are no statutes in the provinces providing at present for the registration of aircraft or of personal property in general. Any amendments required to the conditional sales acts would be to remove aircraft from the kinds of property that might be registered under these acts. In any event, if the legislation as passed by parliament to establish a central aircraft registry was framed so as to be legislation in relation to aeronautics and not in relation to property, I am of opinion that complementary provincial legislation would not be required in order to make it effective.
As I mentioned in my letter of June 30th to you under the rules of procedure of the conference matters are not placed on the agenda unless there is a reasonable likelihood that any model act prepared by the conference will be adopted by at least three provinces. As no provincial legislation apart from possible amendments to the conditional sales act would appear to be required in order to make a central aircraft registry effective in Canada I do not feel any useful purpose would be served in referring this matter to the conference at this time.
Yours sincerely,
Davie Fulton.

I thank you, Mr. Speaker. I should also like to thank the house for the courtesy extended to me. I had perhaps not paced myself too well. Perhaps all I can say is

that the Minister of Transport confirmed basically the opinion that was expressed in this letter to the Minister of Justice. I think that would help to dispose of the jurisdictional question raised by the hon. member for Laurier.
In view of the fact that you want a very brief summation, Mr. Speaker, I think perhaps I should say this. I have tried to indicate as clearly as possible the foundation namely, first of all that the federal government has jurisdiction and second, the necessity for such a central registry. The positive suggestions I should like to make at the present time would be first, to recommend to the Minister of Transport that D.O.T. officials and representatives of Canadian aviation be sent down to Oklahoma city in the United States where the present central registry is located, in order to inspect and subsequently to report on this registry. Second, I would recommend that the Minister of Transport have the department investigate present Canadian registration procedure and see what steps would be required in addition for a central aircraft registry.
Third, I would propose that draft legislation should subsequently be drawn and submitted to a committee of the house and that representations should be requested from the provinces and interested aviation people. I think the growth of air transportation brings me to my final recommendation, and that is something that has been emphasized. In Montreal there is ICAO, the international civil aeronautic organization which is the U.N. central air organization. We have IATA, the international air transport association as world headquarters. In McGill University we have the McGill institute of air and space law. I would suggest that, in conjunction with the recommendations that I have made, it would seem suitable that consideration should be given by the government to uniting all the functions dealing with aeronautics and, I would suggest also, all the functions dealing with outer space-I believe this year Canada will be using a United States vehicle in order to launch her own satellite-and to creating a ministry of air and space which would take in all these functions. The space aspect might perhaps seem to be a little bit premature. However, it should be remembered that Canada has been an active participant in the U.N. committee dealing with outer space and has been one since 1958.
I should like to thank the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate for being able to get me within shooting range, and I should also like to thank the house for providing me with this extra time.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. R. Granger (Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador):
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE CANADIAN AIRCRAFT REGISTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the hon. member for Burn-aby-Richmond and I should like to congratulate him on the thoroughness with which he prepared the statement to which we have just listened. As for myself, may I say that I have a great interest in this matter for a number of reasons. However, I hasten to add that if I am long on interest, I am short on technical knowledge. Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, I would ask you to accept my interest as a reason for my making these remarks rather than my ability to make any profound suggestions with respect to the matter before the house.
There are several reasons for my interest. One is that I come from a province in which air transport is an ever growing necessity. To speak specifically, I may say that my riding is the centre of the aircraft industry in Newfoundland. I refer to Gander. There is no need for me to elaborate, nor is this the time at which to do so, on Gander's place historically in aviation and where it stands today. I might also mention Goose Bay and Labrador. However, the thought to which I should like to give expression is that aircraft are being used more and more in an ever increasing number of fields of endeavour in Newfoundland. The medical health services of the province and the department of health use aircraft. The international Grenfell association needs them. In Labrador they are essential in these respects. Mail is delivered by aircraft in wintertime. Then there is the ordinary conventional use to which aircraft are being put in Newfoundland. I might mention fisheries in particular. There is a growing need for the increased use of aircraft for various purposes. I might add that our province was made for the use of aircraft and that we should like to see aircraft used even more to the betterment of the people.
Those few remarks probably explain the basis of my interest, apart from the personal interest which I have in the use of smaller aircraft. I think of my own personal interest in the flying club association, for instance. However, the fact of the matter is that in the world in which we are living aircraft are being used more and more by governments, corporations and individuals.
I think perhaps the comparison made of aircraft with ships is a fair one or the suggestion that a central registry is needed for aircraft in the same way as one is needed for shipping. Despite the increasing use of aircraft by individuals, by the very nature of their use they still resemble ships more closely than they resemble motor cars. In saying that I am not thinking of the fact that some alight on the land and some on the water. I am thinking of the whole concept

Aeronautics Act
of flying, the use to which aircraft are put and the distance which even the smaller aircraft of today is expected to cover.
As they grow in number the problems which the hon. member seeks to meet through his bill are certainly becoming more acute. We are not dealing with just a few aircraft in an occasional place or in few areas. We are dealing now with a vehicle which is in widespread use throughout the length and breadth of Canada and which promises to come into ever greater use as time goes by. As I say, I think the idea seems to be a sound one in what it wishes to avoid and what it wishes to bring about. However, I must admit that I am speaking as a layman with regard to this problem. At first glance, I think that a central registry for aircraft seems to be a good idea. If I now appear to condemn by faint praise, that does not mean at all that I am against the bill. One or two matters which were raised-and incidentally I may say they were raised by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond when he sought to answer them this afternoon-have not been answered quite to my satisfaction, although it is quite possible that I did not follow him carefully enough or that I misunderstood some of what he said. I think he did very well in pacing himself to keep within his time.
As I said, this matter is a technical one. Last year the hon. member for Laurier raised one objection which the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond sought to answer today. That is the question of whether or not the bill infringes provincial rights. In listening to the hon. member I gathered that he has not yet had replies from one or two provinces, including Newfoundland. I may be mistaken in my interpretation of what he said but it did not seem to me that the arguments he advanced completely met the problem of whether or not the bill is in conflict with provincial jurisdiction. I do not know either, but I think it is one matter that should be thoroughly investigated so that we will know the answer beyond any shadow of doubt before any move is made. Before the bill becomes law and a part of the aeronautics legislation of Canada I think parliament ought to be sure that it is clearly within federal jurisdiction without any conflict whatsoever with provincial rights.
The other suggestion that was made last year was that the bill should go to a committee for complete examination. I believe the hon. member has conceded that point and has said that this should be done. It is quite likely that the objection I have raised as to the possibility of the bill being in conflict with provincial jurisdiction would be dealt with right in that committee. As a matter of

fact, I would assume that a committee studying the bill would make very sure that it was clearly a federal matter. As the hon. member has already suggested that a committee should examine the bill, I believe the criticism I have raised with respect to possible infringement of provincial jurisdiction would be dealt with at that time.
Other than making these two points and emphasizing again the importance of legislation regarding aircraft, there is not much more I wish to say. I would point out that the use of aircraft is growing and unquestionably will continue to grow. Aircraft of various sizes are becoming a common sight in the skies of Canada. There is an increase in private flying which in itself makes this legislation very interesting and legislation to which serious consideration certainly should be given.

speechtext:
According to the Minister of Justice this is an extremely important bill. He said it forms an integral part of the government's national policy. He also spoke of the importance of nationhood in economic matters, which reminds us of the type of comment we were accustomed to hear in 1957.
I refer to the Winnipeg Free Press of April 25, 1957, in which the then leader of the opposition, now Prime Minister of Canada, was reported as speaking about the growing dominance of foreign owned business. He said:
Foreign investment was to be welcomed and should be treated fairly "but a sense of national destiny for Canada calls for it being directed to the maximum benefit of Canada."
At Halifax, on April 26, 1957, he spoke of preserving for Canadians "the control of our economic destiny". Therefore we can presume what basically the government and the minister have in mind when he talks about this being an extremely important bill. It was for that reason that question No. 164 was asked by me, as recorded at page 1241 of Hansard tor February 26, 1962. I asked:
3. 1962
Corporations and Labour Unions
What is the percentage of foreign investment control in the years 1956 and 1961 in (a) the resource industries (b) the manufacturing industries?
The answer given was that the percentage of foreign investment control of the mining and smelting industry increased from 58 per cent in 1956 to 61 per cent in 1959, and that no further figures were available with respect to subsequent years. The answer also stated that the percentage of foreign investment control of manufacturing industries increased from 52 per cent in 1956 to 57 per cent in 1959. Therefore from the figures disclosed by this government it would seem that the policy of 1957 has not been fulfilled. In fact this matter, which the government complained of, has considerably worsened.
Having spoken of this bill as being an extremely important one, the minister went on to say, as reported at page 2399 of Hansard:
-the bill is to some extent experimental and it is, indeed, as I myself recognize, a first step.
We are interested in where this step is going, and what is the purpose of grouping together a corporation and a union in this extraordinary fashion. Is one simply a saw off against the other? Is this simply a propaganda bill which appears to indicate activism on the part of the government in an area where it has already demonstrated marked failure? Is it a case of taking one section of the economy and dealing with it in one section of the bill, and then taking unions and dealing with them in another section, thereby trying to give the appearance of some sort of fair saw off to two elements in our economic society?
It would appear that there is nothing in the bill to indicate to what end the information will be obtained and, as we go through all its clauses, I think we can fairly contend that all the important information is already available to the government or, if it is not, it could be very easily obtained by minor alterations in present requirements. I believe information could easily be obtained by one minister from corporations and by another minister from unions, and that this information would disclose all that was necessary. In fact when he spoke yesterday the minister did not indicate what particular gaps existed in information.
The changes which have taken place in the drafting of this bill in past months have resulted in the presentation of an emasculated bill which is now so innocuous that it will do nothing helpful, nothing indeed except cause obstruction, expense, delay, inconvenience and perhaps some small measure of insult to people endeavouring to carry on business in Canada from the corporate or union standpoint.

Corporations and Labour Unions
I have taken the trouble to discuss it with Mr. Andy Andras of the Canadian Labour Congress and I thought his approach to it was extremely fair. He said there were some minor particulars in which information might be useful, even to the unions themselves, but added that this could be easily obtained in another way.
What is the new intention of the government in taking this first step and where does the second step come in? I invited some opinion on the bill from people who are attached to a school of business administration. One head of a department said that this legislation inserts into the record of parliament a new type of legislation, namely a recordkeeping function that smacks of Hitler. This may sound strange, but hon. members will recall that some years ago Hitler, for reasons that were not very clearly disclosed at that time, required a certain ethnic group to register. What is the reason why these unions must register?
I looked into the records in the parliamentary library and found that there is published by the Department of Labour a pamphlet covering labour organizations in Canada for each year, in very complete detail. I find, on looking through this information, that it is fully documented. I do not think there are any secrets which cause the Minister of Labour any embarrassment in not knowing what are the important unions and who are their executive heads from time to time.
Of course it is a problem to keep completely up to date with respect to unions of a hundred members. In fact, surely no recordkeeping function of the government is ever going to permit this to be completely up to date. It will always be out of date. But the information is always available if the government needs it. In fact it is nearly all available in the publications now printed by the Department of Labour.
What, then, are the mysteries with respect to corporations, or is this simply another indication of fear and displeasure that people who have some relationship outside this country happen to, and are pleased to, come and do business in Canada, either from the management or the labour side? If that is all it is, I think there is much reason for speaking against this bill. It seems to me that this administration has managed to do quite a bit since 1957 to simply discourage investment generally.
A few days ago I was looking at a publication printed by the Bank of Canada for the year 1961 and I found, as I looked at the graphs that appear on page 25 of Mr. Rasminsky's report, that the business fixed capital formation has substantially declined since 1957; that construction is substantially
[Mr. Matheson.I
down; that machinery and equipment is down. Surely this is not the time for us to insert new, picayune legislation which has no real purpose, which the minister himself said is experimental, the first step; but he does not tell us what the second, third or fourth steps really are. We have no idea where this thing is going or what it seeks to accomplish.
Is there a real problem of corporate control? Certainly if we read the press today and project what appears to be the trend, we find in such industries as mining and smelting and manufacturing that there has been a very substantially increased United States ownership in Canada since the year 1959. There have been prognoses by such people as Earle McLaughlin and others who have been interested in certain specialized parts of our economy, such as the monetary and fiscal techniques which have been employed by this government since, for instance, December, 1960 which seem to indicate that the situation has substantially worsened since the baby budget.
If the government does in fact know that their policy in the fiscal or monetary field has tended to bring a good deal more foreign control into our industries, I think the minister should disclose that information. We are vitally interested; that is why we asked the kind of question we did in No. 164: What is the percentage of foreign investment? Does this government have anything further beyond 1959? If it does not, is it alarmed by the substantial increase of foreign investment and control that appeared between 1959 and 1956? Is this government really concerned about increased control from outside this country in labour organization?
We have had no evidence from the minister that this is a fact. We have to bear in mind that as we take this step with Bill C-38 it is certainly a step towards nationalism. In some of his remarks the minister would appear to have indicated that this is not really the purpose; it is not really nationalism. If it is not, I would like to know what it is, because surely we are moving into a time in the world where the tendency among enlightened modern countries who are uplifting their economies is to work together and not against one another. The implements and techniques of national limitation and control are completely contrary to the tempo of development that we see demonstrated, for instance in Europe, Great Britain and the United States, and certainly in Latin America.
Is this just another indication that we are going to go it alone; that we are going to cut off our outside connections which in many ways have elevated not only Canadian development, industry and expansion, particularly

in the speculative areas of our economy, but have also done a good deal, surely, in the labour area? Are we moving alone in this field, having regard to the direction of enlightened progress elsewhere?
I say that reading sympathetically and carefully the obviously very carefully prepared remarks of the minister we do not know where this is going, or why; we do not really have any vice to be corrected; if so the minister has not indicated what it is. If it is to implement what the Prime Minister appeared to indicate to be his policy in 1957, would the minister give us some more facts? Would he tell us the extent to which this government during the last two or three years has really found itself the victim of foreign control and investment. It seems to me manifestly clear, by all the financial statements we can look at, that Canadians are not now of a mind to invest very generously in their own country. It seems to me that in certain areas-and this is certainly true in the mining and smelting industry and Canadian secondary manufacturing-Canadians have not been quick to step forward in recent months to invest in Canada.
What does the minister really mean by "first step"? Surely we are entitled to know something beyond this. We would like to have some idea of what the second step might mean. Does it mean, to cut out foreign investment; does it mean to curtail, limit or prevent the activities of international unions in Canada? If this is the purpose of the government, surely we should know what the government is thinking of as the second or third step phase, because if the second or third step phase is something that tends to be contrary to the trend of progressive development, this is something germane to our discussions at the present time.

If the hon. gentleman would increase the figures so the small companies would not be subjected to the application of this measure, I think I would be very glad to support the amendment. I urge the hon. gentleman to put the ceiling a little higher.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: I am the most agreeable person in the committee this evening. I do not object to raising the limit. Among the hon. member for Hull, the Minister of Justice and the hon. member for Skeena we might amicably agree on a figure of less than $500,000 and unanimously support the amendment. I am in the awkward position of being restricted by the rules from amending my own amendment and that would have to be done by someone else.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: Would $300,000 suit the hon. member?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am not in the
business of auctioning.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: We might put up the hon. member for Assiniboia and the bid could be raised to $400,000.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: Not as far as I am concerned.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: The hon. member for Hull has the opportunity of placing a subamendment before the committee if he is prepared to write it out.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext:
I will put it back to the original figure, Mr. Chairman. I move that paragraph (h) be deleted and replaced with the following which contains the original figures:
(h) any corporation, for any reporting period of the corporation in respect of which it can be established that
(a)	the gross revenue of the corporation for that reporting period from the business carried on by it in Canada, determined as prescribed by the regulations, did not exceed five hundred thousand dollars, and
(b)	the assets in Canada of the corporation as of the last day of that reporting period, determined as prescribed by the regulation, did not exceed two hundred and fifty thousand dollars,
except any such corporation that is one of two or more corporations that, by reason of inter-relationship of management, ownership or financial affairs, are designated by the minister to be related corporations and that would not, if considered as a single corporation, qualify as a corporation described in this item.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: The subamendment reads that paragraph (h) be deleted and replaced by the wording the hon. member has suggested, and it goes on to change the figures from $100,000 to $500,000 in subclause (a) and from $50,000 to $250,000, in subclause (b).

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, would it not be simpler-just to show how co-operative we are here- if my friend the hon. member for Hull wishes to move an amendment, were he merely to move to delete paragraph (h) of the amendment? That would restore the original provision, I believe.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: It would not.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext:
I do not think it would, Mr. Chairman, because the original amendment strikes out the whole of the schedule so there would be nothing left then and all these corporations would be affected if the suggestion of the Minister of Justice were adopted.
I should like to say a word about the amendment moved by my hon. friend. While I can well understand in the original amendment the reason for this, I think the rather compelling observations made by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River about putting an unnecessary charge upon small corporations to provide this information is something that will appeal to everybody in the committee. I think there has been unanimity almost to the point of competition, if unanimity can reach that point, to show that we in the committee are all friends of small business. No person has professed a greater
Corporations and Labour Unions interest in small business than has the leader of the N.D.P. I am sure he could just turn around to his group and suggest to them that we should not seek to penalize small business in an amendment which otherwise is seeking to make great corporations like the Bell Telephone Company and the C.P.R. subject to the law to which the middle size corporations will be subject. I think it would make it a great deal easier to get more support for the amendment if the subamendment commended itself to the leader of the N.D.P. and his followers.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: If I may interrupt the hon. gentleman for a moment, I simply wish to say that we are delighted to see what an influence we are having on the official opposition on a matter such as this one. I wish to correct him in one respect. I wish he would refer to me as parliamentary leader.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: I should be happy to make a bargain with the hon. gentleman since we are in the business of bargaining at the moment. If the hon. gentleman will stop referring to the Leader of the Opposition by an incorrect designation and will call him the Leader of the Opposition, I shall be very glad to call the hon. gentleman almost anything he would like to be called, except leader of the opposition.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: Is the committee ready for the question on the subamendment?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext:
Question.
Amendment to the amendment (Mr. Caron) negatived: yeas, 22; nays, 41.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext:
I declare the
subamendment lost.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: If I may I should like to say a word before the amendment is put. Notwithstanding the fact that our subamendment has been lost because small business appears to have no friends in the Tory party any more-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: -it seems to me that the major aim of the amendment to bring certain of these huge corporations under the same law as that under which ordinary business is put, is the transcendent part. We would have been happier to have it in better form. However, in the circumstances, I would hope that my friends in the chamber would join with me in supporting the amendment.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext:
You have not too many of them.
1,

Corporations and Labour Unions

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: I do not know whether I was included among those to whom the hon. member referred as his friends.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: Not in a political sense.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: That feeling is mutual, in any event. I remember reading some time ago parts out of May's Parliamentary Practice which stated that if an amendment was defeated the original thereby stands. I imagine therefore that we have now voted in favour of the $100,000 and the $50,000 and perhaps we should delete that in putting that amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: My hon. friend by that remark indicates the same knowledge of parliamentary procedure which allowed him yesterday to attempt to mislead the house. I do not think he will succeed in misleading the committee. Now that the opening bargaining and bidding process between the members of the Liberal opposition and the members of the N.D.P. opposition is complete, perhaps we can settle the matter of the amendment on its merits.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: By brute force.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: By this bill we include those giant corporations which have foreign control and about the effect of whose foreign control we know nothing. We exempt only those about whose foreign control we already know.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: You do not know about some of the big ones.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: In spite of the fact that for many years he was parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance, my friend the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River must have occupied his time in that capacity in such a way as to give him none of the information which he could have obtained. However, I can assure him that those to whom the information is available are able to profit by it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: I was familiar with items 1 to 6 every year while I was there.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: Precisely. However, my hon. friend does not seem to have put his familiarization to any good purpose. The point I make is that any further explanation would only be repetition on the ears of those who are not prepared to profit by the information. I therefore suggest that we might take the sense of the committee on the amendment.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext:
I cannot allow to pass without comment the reflections made by the minister on my colleague the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. From a minister who was obliged to confess earlier this evening

that he had not read his speech since January and that it had egregious errors in it, it seems to me the suggestion comes with ill grace that some other hon. member has not read every document he might have read before coming into the chamber.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext:
I would appreciate it, Mr. Chairman, if henceforth the Minister of Justice would refer to us here as the effective opposition. He would then be more nearly correct. However, I would point out this, if I could inferentially make reference to that about which the minister spoke and also to something which was attempted yesterday. My interpretation of the rules is that it succeeded. I am not one of those, as was the minister last year, who deliberately refuses to carry out his obligations under an act of parliament merely because he disagrees with what the results might be.
The Depuiy Chairman: Is the committee ready for the question on the amendment?

speechtext:

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, before you put clause 3 to a vote, I would point out that while the bill was given second reading without a division and it might therefore be said that it was supported unanimously, nevertheless it is a type of bill in which there is a mixture of goodness and badness. Members are often put in the position in dealing with bills of agreeing to second reading in the hope that in the committee stage the forcefulness of their arguments will have some effect on the minister involved from the point of view of increasing the effectiveness of the bill and improving upon it. With clause 3 as it now stands I will only say in passing that if we are unable to effect any alterations in the schedule when we are dealing with it paragraph by paragraph I am in serious doubt what my action will be on third reading. At the present moment my feeling is that I will not be able to support the bill on third reading if it reaches that stage in the same form it is now.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, when we come to clause 4 of the bill we will see-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: Are we on clause 4?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext:
No; I am simply referring to it in connection with the question I am going to ask. When we come to that clause we will see that there are two sections to the return that is going to be required. In the schedule there are a number of types of companies listed. Under the statutes under which these companies operate are they

obliged to make returns in two parts, one part confidential and the other part not confidential?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: I think that would vary from case to case. Perhaps my hon. friend would ask me about particular cases. Generally speaking, however, the corporations enumerated in the first six paragraphs of the schedule report in very great detail. I am advised, for instance, that each insurance company reports in a great thick volume to the superintendent of insurance. The superintendent of insurance in turn, in the same way as the dominion statistician will do here with respect to part B returns, publishes his annual report summarizing the effects of the various individual reports he has had from the insurance companies in Canada. It is very much the same sort of system as will be followed under this bill.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: Is there any part of the reports now being made to the transport commission or other bodies which is comparable to the section B confidential reports we are asking these other companies to make?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: Yes, indeed, Mr. Chairman. All the financial statements of the banks, insurance companies, trust companies, loan companies and so on, required to be filed with the respective officers detailed in the statutes under which they operate, are very much comparable to the financial information that will be required to be filed under this part.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: Are they considered as confidential now?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: Yes, I understand that the details of the returns are confidential generally speaking in the case of the officers with whom they are filed, just as the details of the returns under part B will be confidential; but an analysis is made and a report summarizing the effects of all the information received is made by, for instance, the superintendent of insurance, just as a report compiled by the dominion bureau of statistics will be made in this case.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: As it stands now, the small loans companies report to the Department of Finance under the Small Loans Act. Is there a part of their reports which is now considered confidential under the statute?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext:
I am informed that the details of financial statements, in such detail as is required under the Small Loans Act, that are filed with the Department of Finance would not be made available in detail to the public, but that there is no statutory or other bar to the revealing of that information in detail to the government in order that the government
Business of the House
may decide upon the policy that should be followed with respect to small loans companies.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: Who decides which part should be confidential and which part should not be confidential?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: That would be determined, I think, by virtue of the act under which the companies report. This bill will determine which parts of the report are confidential and which are not.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: Then why are we asking more from other companies than we are asking from those included in the schedule? That is another reason why they should all be under the same act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: Again I say I am advised that in the case of the insurance companies particularly, and most of the companies in the first six paragraphs of the schedule, they report a great deal more detail than the companies under this bill will be required to report.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext:
But there is nothing in the law
which says that part of it shall be confidential. It is only the department which decides which part shall be confidential.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: No, I have just pointed out that according to my understanding it is the respective statutes under which they report which determine what and to what extent confidentiality will be preserved.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext:
I was told a while ago that in
the case of the small loans companies the department decides what should be confidential and that there is nothing in the statute in that regard.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: If I understood correctly, the minister said earlier that the returns of those companies that are exempt under this legislation because they report somewhere else will be available to the bureau of statistics.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FURNISHING OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER STATISTICS
speechtext: Oh, yes. There is no bar whatsoever on the conveying of information within the government.
